candidates.title: Targeting G protein-coupled receptor networks for healthy aging: grounding systems geroprotection in biophysical and data realities
candidates.abstract: In their lead article in Frontiers in Science, Boeringer et al. propose targeting networks of G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) as a promising strategy for geroprotection (Boeringer et al. 2026). This approach builds on the remarkable versatility of GPCRs, which sense a wide range of extracellular signals, engage diverse signaling pathways, are broadly expressed across tissues, and play important roles in many disease processes. By framing the GPCRome as a central, druggable regulator of multiple hallmarks of aging, from inflammaging and mitochondrial dysfunction to stem cell depletion, the authors advance an intriguing hypothesis in which systems pharmacology could be used to rebalance several of these processes simultaneously, potentially delaying the onset of chronic disease and extending healthspan. The proposed integration of artificial intelligence (AI), digital twins, and quantum computing to rationally manipulate such complex signaling networks is bold and thought-provoking.At the same time, translating this compelling vision into therapeutic reality presents formidable biophysical, computational, and experimental challenges. The authors explicitly acknowledge several of these limitations, including the sparsity and variable quality of available training data, the context dependence of GPCR signaling, and, importantly, the fact that network-and AI-guided polypharmacology does not yet constitute a validated or generalizable framework for designing multi-receptor interventions. Several further considerations may help define what will be required to move this exciting concept from a compelling systems-level hypothesis toward an experimentally testable and ultimately translatable framework for GPCR network pharmacology.The proposed networks contain many receptors with established disease relevance, but deciding that a receptor belongs in an aging network does not tell us how it should be modulated. A therapeutic network requires knowing whether a receptor should be activated, inhibited, partially activated, allosterically modulated, biased toward one effector, or manipulated in a tissue-restricted manner, and by how much. This distinction matters because GPCR effects are strongly dependent on receptor density, coupling repertoire, accessory proteins, cellular state, ligand concentration, and tissue context.Especially problematic is the situation for biased ligands. Compared with binding data, efficacy data are sparse and functional measurements are not interchangeable across assays.A ligand that appears biased in one cellular background may not retain the same functional preference in another because receptor expression levels, membrane lipid composition, expression reserve, transducer abundance, signal amplification, and regulatory machinery differ. Consequently, pooling efficacy measurements from heterogenous assays may obscure the underlying pharmacology and limit the predictive utility of models trained on such data.The challenge, therefore, is not simply to assemble more data, but to assemble the right data, including their experimental context.The proposed GPCRome is necessarily constrained by measurements reported in the literature. This creates an important circularity: well-studied receptors become highly connected nodes, while poorly characterized receptors, including orphan receptors (i.e., receptors without known endogenous or synthetic ligands) or incompletely deorphanized GPCRs, may be absent or misrepresented despite mediating potentially important biology, leaving major blind spots in any GPCRome network reconstruction. Boeringer et al. also highlight receptors for which human or translational evidence remains limited, with several proposed nodes supported primarily by in vitro cellular assays and animal models. It remains uncertain whether network topologies derived from controlled rodent experiments will reproduce the networks operating in complex, heterogeneous human populations.A useful next step would therefore be a community-wide effort to construct a standardized, machine-readable GPCR functional atlas. But the harder question is what such an atlas should actually measure, as binding affinity alone is insufficient. Harmonized measurements of ligand association and dissociation, receptor expression and activation, G-protein coupling, β-arrestin engagement, pathway-specific efficacy, receptor trafficking and internalization, desensitization, and signaling duration, are urgently needed-ideally across multiple physiologically relevant cellular backgrounds. Rather than reducing heterogeneous experiments to a single activity label, negative results and experimental metadata should be collected as well, and ideally shared in standardized, accessible format. Such a resource could make network inference more robust and, importantly, reveal where uncertainty really lies. While ligands reshape populations of GPCR conformations, different transducers both select receptor states and undergo their own conformational changes. Thus, signaling cannot be reduced to a ligand-induced receptor state. Rather, AI-based structure prediction, molecular dynamics and enhanced sampling, structural biology, and biophysical measurements should be considered complementary approaches for characterizing receptor-transducer conformational ensembles (Wootten et al., 2013;Hilger et al., 2018).Kinetics adds another critical dimension. Ligand residence time, receptor activation and deactivation rates, trafficking and recycling, and the duration of downstream signaling may influence in vivo efficacy and therapeutic window beyond what is captured by equilibrium affinity or endpoint efficacy (Copeland et al., 2006). Incorporating these temporal features into network models could improve both the selection of network-level interventions and the prediction of physiological outcomes.Sparse data should not necessarily halt progress, but they should change the modeling strategy. Transfer learning offers a particularly attractive route: models can learn shared representations from data-rich GPCRs and then adapt to understudied receptors, provided that domain differences and uncertainty are explicitly modeled [e.g., (Provasi and Filizola, 2025)]. The goal should not be to manufacture confidence from sparse data, but to quantify uncertainty and use it to prioritize the next experiment. AI can then become an activelearning engine linking prediction to targeted measurements rather than a one-way generator of hypotheses (Nguyen et al., 2024).A related issue is chemical space. Much of the historical GPCR ligand repertoire was optimized for individual targets, not for deliberately engineered polypharmacology. The chemical matter already available to the field may therefore be a poor representation of the multitarget molecules needed for network control. While generative modeling architectures have successfully enabled the exploration of new regions of chemical space, the objective should be defined in terms of multi-receptor and multi-pathway pharmacology, including selectivity, efficacy, kinetics, tissue exposure, and safety, rather than simply potency at one receptor. This is where structure-based methods, functional profiling, generative chemistry, and experimental validation need to be tightly coupled.Perhaps the most important question is whether the proposed network architecture will have translational relevance. Boeringer et al. (Boeringer et al. 2026) present mechanistic hypotheses that draw largely on cellular studies, animal models, and selected examples of clinical pharmacology. However, networks inferred from preclinical systems may look quite different in patients, where age, genotype, comorbidities, medication history, tissue composition, and disease stage can all reshape signaling. The authors' vision of digital twins and patient-specific GPCR interventions is compelling precisely because it points to this missing layer.The next step should be to test these network hypotheses directly against patient-derived data rather than assume that preclinical networks represent stable therapeutic maps. Single-cell and spatial transcriptomics, proteomics, functional biomarkers, clinical phenotypes, and longitudinal treatment-response data could help establish which receptor nodes are conserved in humans and which are specific to particular tissues. Ultimately, the goal should not be to build a larger GPCR network, but a better-calibrated one that makes predictions that can be rigorously tested, challenged, and ultimately falsified in patients.A major strength of the Boeringer et al. article is that it challenges the field to think beyond the single receptor. That is an important conceptual shift. The next challenge is not simply to add more receptors, but to establish the experimental and computational standards needed to make network pharmacology genuinely testable. Such a program would: combine systematic, context-rich functional measurements with patient-derived evidence; use approaches such as transfer learning and uncertainty-aware active learning to deal with sparse data; account for receptor-transducer mechanisms and signaling kinetics rather than relying on static structures alone; and integrate physics-based and data-driven approaches to connect molecular mechanisms with cellular and organismal behavior (Hendrickx et al., 2020).The central question, then, is whether we can generate the data, assays, models, and chemical tools needed to perturb these networks in a predictable way. Turning this framework into something clinically useful will require considerably more experimental grounding and validation than the current computational roadmap implies.diseases might eventually become. But moving from theoretical network diagrams to clinically useful geroprotective therapeutics will require computational models firmly grounded in experimental biophysics and human biology. No single computational or experimental approach will be sufficient. What is needed instead is an integrated framework that brings together community-generated harmonized functional data, kinetic profiling, mechanistic modeling, generative chemistry, and patient-derived evidence. The real measure Filizola, M. Realities of GPCR Network Control 9 of success will not be how comprehensive the resulting GPCR networks appear, but whether they capture signaling well enough to generate predictions that can be experimentally tested and, ultimately, translated to patients.The author declared that generative AI was used in the creation of this manuscript.ChatGPT.Edu (GPT 5.6 Sol) was used to assist with editing. The author remains responsible for checking the factual accuracy of the manuscript and for the final content.

candidates.title: Optimal-transport flow matching for stochastic model ipdating
candidates.abstract: Deep generative models have attracted considerable attention as inference engines for stochastic model updating. Among these deep generative models, conditional flow matching offers a particularly efficient formulation, in which a continuous transport map from a latent distribution to the posterior is learned by regression against optimal-transport probability paths, avoiding both the invertibility constraints of normalising flows and the iterative denoising of diffusion models. However, its performance in engineering model updating has not been examined against an established baseline such as the Bayesian updating framework under controlled conditions. In this work, conditional flow matching is therefore assessed against the Bayesian model updating approach with transitional Markov chain Monte Carlo, in which the Bhattacharyya distance provides the approximate likelihood for the Bayesian approach. The two methods are assessed with respect to posterior fidelity, evaluated by statistical distances against the known ground truth and computational expenditure in model evaluations, with the offline training budget reported separately from the inference cost of each subsequent conditioning. A 3-DOF spring–mass system with uncertain stiffness parameters serves as the benchmark. Since the calibrated posterior constitutes the input description upon which subsequent reliability assessment depends, the accuracy and the marginal cost of the updating step both bear directly on reliability computations. In addition, the amortised nature of the learned transport map is discussed in this work, as it permits the posterior to be re-evaluated under new observations at negligible cost, which is a property of practical relevance to reliability assessment under sequentially acquired monitoring data.

candidates.title: Predicting Ternary Complex Stability through Binding Free-Energy Calculations in the Geometric Route
candidates.abstract: Abstract Molecular glue-induced targeted protein degradation is a powerful emerging therapeutic modality that exploits the ubiquitin-proteasome degradation pathway to break down proteins associated with disease proliferation. At the structural level, degradation proceeds through the formation of a ternary complex induced by small molecules between the target protein and an E3 ligase. Unlike PROTACs, molecular glues do not require a chemical linker and tend to stabilize preexisting native protein–protein interactions. Computational screening of novel glues is challenging, in large part due to the complexity and high degree of cooperativity involved in the formation of the ternary complex interface. Here, we present a rigorous Molecular Dynamics-based simulation protocol that uses Umbrella Sampling to calculate the ternary complex binding free energy. The protocol follows a geometric thermodynamic cycle with conformational and Boresch-style orientational restraints to drive the system from bound to unbound. Our framework successfully predicts the effect of single-point interface mutations on the relative stability of the CK1α-lenalidomide-CRBN ternary complex (R2 = 0.95 compared to experimental binding affinities). We also study a series of systems related to the BRD4 degraders IBG1 and IBG3, which recruit the DCAF16 E3 ligase. We rank various complexes engaging DCAF16 by their binding free energies and achieve an ordering that is consistent with the trends observed in biophysical assays. Of particular note is our ability to assert the reliance of BRD4 selectivity on a single interfacial glycine residue, which alternative, reduced-sampling MM/GBSA or HADDOCK scoring methodologies fail to achieve. Overall, our protocol shows promise as a generalizable approach to ranking ternary complexes by thermodynamic stability, potentially aiding in the identification of potent new degraders.

candidates.title: Geometric decomposition of information flow for overdamped Langevin systems and optimal transport in subsystems
candidates.abstract: Information flow between subsystems is a central concept in information thermodynamics, which provides the second-law-like inequalities for subsystems. This paper discusses the geometric decomposition of information flow, which was introduced for Markov jump systems [Physical Review Research, 8, 023292 (2026)], and applies it to overdamped Langevin systems. For overdamped Langevin systems, the geometric decomposition of information flow into excess and housekeeping contributions is related to the conventional definition of the 2-Wasserstein distance between marginal distributions in optimal transport theory. This formulation offers an optimal-transport interpretation of subsystem dynamics, and this optimal-transport formulation is simpler for overdamped Langevin systems than for general Markov jump systems. It is also possible to handle features that are specific to overdamped Langevin systems, such as representations based on the Koopman mode decomposition, as well as their relationship with the Fisher information matrix. As with the results for Markov jump systems, we generalize the second law of information thermodynamics using housekeeping and excess information flow, leading to the concepts of excess and housekeeping demons. We also derive a thermodynamic uncertainty relation and an information-thermodynamic speed limit incorporating excess information flow. These results are illustrated for the Gaussian case, and we discuss the conditions under which the excess and housekeeping demons emerge.

candidates.title: Learning Protein-Protein Interaction Interfaces from Multimodal Representations
candidates.abstract: Background: Protein-protein interactions govern essential cellular processes, making the identification of interface residues critical for protein engineering and molecular design. Although complex deep learning algorithms like AlphaFold3 generate full atom resolution assemblies, they are not optimized for residue-level interface identification. Existing methods face inherent limitations: sequence-based models lack explicit 3D context, while structure-based approaches can overlook evolutionary signals. Results: By combining evolutionary context with 3D geometry, the multimodal protein language model ESM3 offers the ideal foundation for residue-level interface classification. This results in the ESM3-PPISites model, which outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods across diverse training and benchmark sets. Generalization is assessed through stringent sequence- and structure-based redundancy filtering to ensure evaluation on previously unseen proteins. Notably, finetuning the open-weight ESM3 architecture meaningfully narrows the performance gap with its proprietary full-scale counterpart. Furthermore, integrating predicted interaction sites as spatial restraints into HADDOCK significantly improves the recovery of near-native binding poses while reducing computational search time by an order of magnitude compared with blind docking. Conclusions: ESM3-PPISites enables accurate interfaces identification without relying on complex structural inputs at inference time, establishing a reliable and computationally efficient strategy for mapping protein-protein interaction sites.

candidates.title: Deciphering the Structure-Activity Relationships Underpinning the Linkerology of Bivalent EGFR Inhibitors.
candidates.abstract: Linking small molecules that bind adjacent sites on a target is a promising strategy for developing compounds with tight binding affinities. ATP-allosteric bivalent inhibitors (AABIs) of the epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) have provided new insights into efficient linker design where large potency gains can be achieved through particular design scenarios. In this work, we systematically evaluated the structure-activity relationships of target molecules to better understand the most effective approach to maximizing potency through linker optimization. Our results show that linker length and points of connection are both important strategies for significant potency enhancements. Structures and simulations indicate that maximal flexibility is likely the most important design criterion for linking molecules that occupy adjacent pockets, as modeled by the EGFR kinase domain. These studies provide a general framework for the rational design of linkers broadly relevant to fragment-based drug discovery and a number of related scenarios in medicinal chemistry.

candidates.title: SABLE: Scalable Affine Bayesian Latent-space Exploration
candidates.abstract: Complex objects such as engineering designs and proteins are often difficult to optimise because their design spaces exhibit high-dimensional structure and objective evaluations are expensive. Generative models provide continuous latent representations, but their latent spaces can have thousands to tens of thousands of dimensions, creating a regime where the latent dimension $D$ greatly exceeds the evaluation budget. We introduce SABLE, a Bayesian optimisation method for high-dimensional latent spaces with an isotropic distribution and limited budget. SABLE uses a Bayesian affine surrogate for prediction and acquisition, treating higher-order structure as surrogate discrepancy. After $N$ observations, the slope update has dimension at most $N-1$, yielding a decomposition of each query into an in-span component optimised by expected improvement (EI) in at most $N$ dimensions and an off-span component governed by a scalar norm. We show that the off-span norm implicitly selected by affine EI can lead to underexploration, and SABLE instead prescribes it using a finite-horizon schedule, without restricting search to a learned subspace. A recompression scheme reduces information to $\mathcal O(M)$ pseudo-observations, bounding refitting cost by $\mathcal O(M^2D+M^3)$ while keeping parameter inference, prediction, and acquisition decisions to tens of milliseconds. Across synthetic benchmarks and latent-space optimisation tasks, SABLE achieves high sample efficiency and reduces decision time by several orders of magnitude at large budgets.

candidates.title: Causal Chain of Thought: Mitigating Attention Leakage via Context Isolation
candidates.abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting elicits step-by-step rationales that appear to explain model predictions, but there is no guarantee these steps causally drive the final answer. In standard autoregressive generation, dense attention allows each reasoning step to attend to the full context, enabling the model to derive answers through direct lookup while generating plausible-sounding but post-hoc justifications. We introduce CausalCoT, an inference framework that enforces causal transparency by decomposing problems into a directed acyclic graph of atomic sub-questions, evaluating each node in an isolated context containing only its direct causal parents. This Markovian structure removes attention pathways to non-parent content, making downstream predictions sensitive to local reasoning rather than global context leakage. Across a diverse suite of reasoning benchmarks, CausalCoT preserves competitive predictive performance while improving explanation faithfulness, increasing causal sensitivity of intermediate reasoning steps by an average of 12 and up to 21 percentage points over the strongest baseline. The structured dependency graph additionally enables test-time interventions in which local corrections propagate predictably through downstream reasoning.

candidates.title: GenTile: Closing the Loop Between LLM Reasoning and Physical Telemetry for Autonomous NPU Graph Tuning
candidates.abstract: Abstract Large language model (LLM) hidden widths—such as the 18 944-dimensional intermediate layer of the Qwen family—are often burst-aligned but not tile-compatible with heterogeneous NPU Cube engines, forcing the compiler to emit a small residual kernel that stalls the pipeline for up to 77% of cycles. Manual tuning does not scale across the growing space of model dimensions, sequence lengths, and operator variants. We present GenTile, a dual-role Research–Development (R&D) agent framework that closes the loop between LLM causal reasoning and on-device telemetry: a Research agent diagnoses bottlenecks from structured profiles, a Development agent materializes hardware-legal descriptors from compiler feedback, and iteration traces accumulate into a reusable knowledge base under an air-gap sandbox. On Ascend 910B, an offline hardware-faithful sandbox loop first demonstrates convergence mechanics; on real pretrained weights, the loop then measures the full multi-objective trade-off—latency, energy, memory, AICore efficiency, and approximation error (ε)—across six projection families from two Qwen generations (Qwen3.5-32B and Qwen2.5-7B). From telemetry alone, the agent deploys lossless sibling-projection fusions (QKV, gate–up) consistent with production inference-engine layouts (1.06–1.16× faster, up to 13% lower energy, ε=0, stable across sequence lengths, layer depths, and both models), and rejects every lossy low-rank rewrite—including a 1.39× lm_head speedup whose measured ε=0.89 exceeds any usable accuracy budget—while validating the Eckart–Young cliff prediction (ε → 0.002 at the tail rank) on structural layers. Baselines, ablations, cross-dimension generalization, and a sandbox loop that matches the geometric Oracle within four generations without exhaustive search further support the framework.

candidates.title: PI-STGNN model-driven risk assessment method for leapfrog tripping in photovoltaic power plants
candidates.abstract: Unintended fault propagation in photovoltaic plants stems primarily from collector-line leapfrog tripping, a hazard characterized by multi-factor coupling, time-varying dynamics and hidden causal links that remain difficult to fully characterize under complex operating conditions. To tackle this challenge, this work presents a physics-informed spatio-temporal graph neural network (PI-STGNN) tailored for leapfrog tripping risk assessment: a hierarchical indicator set is constructed through systematic analysis of tripping mechanisms and protection coordination rules, a conditional diffusion model is deployed to generate multi-scenario augmented samples to alleviate real-world fault data scarcity, and physical constraints including protection time grading and electrical distance are explicitly embedded into the learning pipeline to strengthen the model’s capacity to capture risk evolution patterns and support accurate identification. For high-risk detection, the proposed approach achieves a precision of 0.92 and a recall of 0.91, delivering a notable reduction in missed detection of high-risk events.

candidates.title: Digital Twin-Assisted Physics-Informed Graph Neural Network Framework with Explainable Artificial Intelligence for Personalized Drug Delivery Optimization
candidates.abstract: The growing demand for personalized drug delivery necessitates intelligent computational approaches that can jointly analyze molecular characteristics, biological targets, physicochemical properties, and therapeutic responses.This study presents a Digital Twin-Assisted Physics-Informed Graph Neural Network (PI-GNN) integrated with Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) to facilitate drug-target response prediction and personalized therapeutic optimization.The proposed framework was developed using 52,274 drug-target interaction records, partitioned into 36,592 training, 5,227 validation, and 10,455 testing samples.Molecular structures were transformed into graphs characterized by 23 atom-level and six bond-level features, while protein sequences were represented through 24 biological attributes.Eight physicochemical parameters-molecular weight, LogP, topological polar surface area (TPSA), hydrogen-bond donors, hydrogen-bond acceptors, rotatable bonds, ring count, and fraction Csp3-were incorporated to provide physics-informed constraints to the learning process.Experimental evaluation on the log-transformed response yielded an R² of 0.4209, RMSE of 2.2985, and MAE of 1.5695 for the test dataset.Permutation-based XAI revealed TPSA as the dominant physicochemical contributor, with its perturbation increasing RMSE by 0.1662 and decreasing R² by 0.0868, followed by molecular weight, LogP, ring count, and hydrogen-bond donors.Molecular-level interpretability was further established using GNNExplainer to identify influential atoms associated with individual predictions.Input-ablation analysis showed that suppressing physicochemical and protein information reduced R² from 0.4209 to -5.0589 and 0.3276, respectively, indicating that the trained network relied substantially on these complementary information sources.The XAI-guided digital-twin module evaluated 10,661 valid molecular candidates, with 5,756 satisfying the specified drug-like constraints.For the selected biological target context, Drug ID 1049 was identified as the highest-ranked candidate, increasing the predicted log-response from 8.5935 to 15.5521, representing an 80.98% relative improvement on the modelled log-response scale and achieving a digital-twin score of 0.8905.Overall, the findings indicate that combining graph-based molecular learning with physicochemical knowledge, model explainability, and digital-twin-driven candidate screening offers an interpretable computational strategy for prioritizing promising drug-target configurations.The framework provides a foundation for subsequent experimental validation and the development of data-driven personalized drug-delivery systems.

candidates.title: DCAF: Unifying Data Validity, Evaluation Validity and Predictive Modeling for Single-cell Perturbation Simulation
candidates.abstract: Single-cell perturbation profiling is limited by cost and throughput, while computational methods remain constrained by inconsistent evaluation and underperformance relative to simple baselines. Here we present DCAF, a unified framework for single-cell perturbation simulation that that jointly addresses data validity, evaluation validity and predictive modeling. Among its three components, DCAF-data addresses the single-measurement limitation by reconstructing pre- and post-perturbation status using entropy-regularized optimal transport, and is demonstrated on both cell line and multi-cell type datasets. DCAF-criterion evaluates log fold changes in non-silenced genes to improve sensitivity to model error and robustness to zero inflation noise, validated on synthetic datasets. DCAF-model combines JEPA with explicit modeling for regulatory-dynamics modeling for interpretable prediction. Across benchmarks, DCAF outperforms state-of-the-art deep-learning methods, as well as mean and linear baselines in cross-gene, cross-cell-type and cross-region generalization. In adult Mouse brain, DCAF recapitulates known cell-type-specific regulatory heterogeneity of Dgcr8 knockdown at both cell type and gene levels. DCAF thus provides a rigorous and biologically grounded foundation for reliable perturbation simulation across development, disease and therapeutic discovery.

candidates.title: Sequence-based artificial intelligence-guided inhibitory peptides to counteract AAV neutralizing antibodies in gene therapy.
candidates.abstract: Adeno-associated virus (AAV) vectors have demonstrated strong clinical efficacy across multiple monogenic disorders, yet neutralizing antibodies (NAbs) remain major barriers to vector redosing and durable transduction. To address this limitation, we developed a sequence-based artificial intelligence framework integrating Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers (BERT) and Evolutionary Scale Modeling with Low-Rank Adaptation (ESM-LoRA) to identify human-tolerant, virus-specific motifs across human and viral proteins using sliding-window analyses and multi-layer fine-tuning. Using capsid-derived segments from AAV2 and AAV843, we prioritized surface-accessible, virus-polarized peptides as candidate decoys and evaluated their ability to block AAV-targeted antibodies. The models achieved high accuracy in distinguishing human versus viral fragments, and selected peptides bound AAV-specific antibodies with nanomolar affinity, competitively restored capsid binding, and recovered >60% of baseline transduction in the presence of NAbs. In mouse models with pre-existing or redosing-induced antibodies, coadministration of decoy peptides and an IgG-degrading enzyme reduced high-titer NAbs to approximately 1:4 and restored hepatic transgene expression without detectable inflammatory or peptide-specific immune responses. A contrastive variational autoencoder (VAE) further generated non-natural peptides with broader epitope coverage. These results support sequence-driven AI design of short, low-immunogenicity decoy peptides as a translational strategy to mitigate NAb interference and enhance the feasibility of AAV redosing.

candidates.title: Questioning Instrumental Convergence in RLVR: Checkpoint Evidence from OLMo-3
candidates.abstract: Instrumental convergence is often invoked as a general reason to expect capable agents to acquire or express power-seeking subgoals: self-preservation, resource acquisition, deception, or resistance to oversight which poses an important threat to the society. For LLMs, reinforcement learning is the first stage of post-training that directly optimizes behavior against an objective; therefore, it is the stage where convergent instrumental behavior, on IC grounds, likely to appear. Does reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) make a model more likely to express instrumental-convergence behavior, or does this depend on the training regime, evaluation frame, and stage of post-training? We study this question as a checkpoint-conditioned behavioral trajectory rather than as a single before/after safety score. Using InstrumentalEval, we evaluate OLMo-3-7B-Think across SFT, DPO, 13 intermediate RLVR checkpoints, and the final RLVR model. The trajectory is nonmonotonic: instrumental rate rises from 25.0% at SFT to 46.1% near RLVR step 200, then falls to 11.8% at the final checkpoint. Paired item-level tests and step-wise regression support the final SFT-to-RLVR reduction. Prompt framing does not explain this pattern: a harmful-prompt indicator combined with other framing effects explains only 15% of within-checkpoint score variance on average, and Iterative Null-space Projection (INLP) removes a detectable framing direction without changing the SFT-to-final-RLVR gap. Together with preliminary 32B endpoint results (35.53% SFT to 22.37% RLVR final), these findings indicate that RLVR does not monotonically increase instrumental behavior in this setting: the rate rises early, then falls below the SFT baseline. The result is specific to this model family and benchmark, and judge agreement is moderate, so absolute rates should be read cautiously.

candidates.title: Fast Solution Methods for the Classical 0–1 Knapsack Problem
candidates.abstract: The classical 0--1 knapsack problem is among the simplest integer programs to state and among the most instructive problems for understanding why algorithm selection must follow instance structure. An input contains items with positive integer weights and profits, and the task is to choose a maximum-profit subset whose total weight does not exceed a capacity. The problem is weakly NP-hard, yet many large instances are solved quickly because exact algorithms exploit moderate numeric parameters, strong linear relaxations, dominance relations, or a small set of uncertain variables near the fractional break item. This review develops a theory-guided account of the principal fast solution methods for the classical problem. It proves the correctness and complexity of weight-indexed and profit-indexed dynamic programming, explains sparse Pareto-frontier implementations and reconstruction, derives the fractional-knapsack upper bound used by branch-and-bound methods, and establishes the correctness of meet-in-the-middle search. It then presents the core concept that underlies influential practical solvers and gives a detailed proof of the standard profit-scaling fully polynomial-time approximation scheme. Modern advances based on structured min-plus convolution are placed within this classical landscape rather than treated as isolated results. The central conclusion is that there is no universally fastest knapsack algorithm. Small item counts favor meet-in-the-middle search, moderate capacities or total profits favor dynamic programming, favorable density structure favors core-based exact methods, and very large numeric coefficients favor approximation. A final decision framework translates these theoretical distinctions into an implementable solver-selection policy while identifying open questions concerning adaptivity, certified switching among methods, memory efficiency, and realistic hard-instance generation.

candidates.title: Reliable AI-Assisted Decisions via Selective Auditing
candidates.abstract: We consider online monitoring of an AI system that produces a sequence of decisions. At each round, the system outputs a proposed decision together with a confidence score estimating the trustworthiness of the decision. The decision and confidence score need not be produced by the same model: for example, one agent may propose a decision, while a separate verifier agent evaluates it and outputs a correctness or safety score. Based on this information, we must decide whether to accept the AI decision automatically or consult an expert, such as a human auditor, who reviews the proposal and either accepts or corrects it. We formulate this task as an online constrained optimization problem in which the goal is to minimize the frequency of expert auditing while guaranteeing that the fraction of AI errors that go unaudited stays below a user-defined threshold. We derive a family of algorithms with provable error-control guarantees with no assumptions, including a method that is optimally efficient: it asymptotically attains the best achievable auditing rate for both adversarial and i.i.d. data streams. Experiments on screening harmful requests to large language models, qualitative text annotation, and data labeling show that our methods achieve valid error control in practice while substantially reducing the need for human auditing compared to baselines.

candidates.title: POMs‐GibbsNet: A Deep Neural Network for the Prediction of Thermodynamic Parameters of Polyoxometalates
candidates.abstract: ABSTRACT Polyoxometalates (POMs) are versatile metal–oxo clusters with remarkable structural diversity and applications spanning catalysis, energy storage, and materials science. However, accurately predicting their thermodynamic properties remains computationally demanding due to the large system sizes and the cost of density functional theory (DFT) frequency calculations required to obtain Gibbs free energies. In this work, we present POMs‐GibbsNet, a deep neural network designed to predict the thermal free energy correction () of polyoxometalates by combining graph‐based molecular representations with DFT‐derived descriptors. Molecular structures were encoded using variants of the AABBA autocorrelation graph kernel, which captures atom–atom, bond–bond, and atom–bond correlations together with quantum‐derived features including QTAIM descriptors. POMs‐GibbsNet was trained on a dataset of 1419 POM structures spanning 19 chemical systems to obtain good results ( and RMSE = 1.9 kcal mol −1 . To evaluate the performance, a benchmark against 10 classical regressors was performed. Additionally, an uncertainty study was added to the methodology. External validation using POMSimulator reaction networks comprising over 10,819 reactions shows excellent agreement between predicted and DFT reaction energies (), with errors typically within a few kcal mol −1 . Error cancellation was also studied during this step. Notably, simplified atom–atom autocorrelation descriptors already provide robust performance while reducing model complexity. These results demonstrate that POMs‐GibbsNet enables efficient estimation of thermodynamic corrections in POM systems, providing a powerful framework for accelerating the computational exploration of polyoxometalate speciation and self‐assembly across large chemical spaces.

candidates.title: Diffusion Language Models for Perplexity-Aware Black-Box Attacks
candidates.abstract: \emph{Continuous-space} attacks find prompts that trigger malicious behaviors, such as overthinking, in black-box LLMs by sampling or optimizing over a low-dimensional Gaussian latent space and decoding it to text through a \emph{random mapping} and nearest-token lookup. Because the random mapping is not learned from language, its prompts can be highly unnatural, and as such easily detectable through input guardrails, and the risk estimates they yield are not grounded in natural prompts. In this paper, we demonstrate that the same continuous latent-space framework can be coupled directly to a learned generative distribution over language, a continuous diffusion language model (dLLM), which removes the artificial random mapping while preserving the standard-Gaussian latent formulation and the downstream sampling or optimization procedure. We evaluate this approach under two settings: sampling-based estimation using \emph{RareTrap} and optimization-based search using \emph{ThinkTrap}. We find that character-level perplexity drops from $10^3$--$10^7$ to 3--5 in RareTrap and from 20--28 to 4.3--5.4 in ThinkTrap. We also find that model risk estimates can differ by an order of magnitude across the two mappings.

candidates.title: METTA: Memory-Enhanced Test-Time Adaptation for Meta-Reinforcement Learning
candidates.abstract: Meta-reinforcement learning aims to train agents that adapt quickly to unseen tasks from limited interaction, but this requires representing task evidence over long interaction histories. Classical recurrent agents compress experience into hidden states, while transformer-based agents retrieve from past trajectories at quadratic memory and computation cost. In this work, we propose Memory-Enhanced Test-Time Adaptation (METTA) for meta-reinforcement learning. It decomposes the fast adaptation phase into two temporal scales: a causal neural memory performs fine-grained within-episode adaptation with linear sequence complexity, while compact episode-level summaries support long-range cross-episode task inference without attending over the full interaction history. Moreover, equipping agents with neural memory provides sufficient expressive capacity and test-time training capability, enabling effective adaptation to unseen held-out tasks and task families at meta-test time. On unseen held-out Meta-World ML10/45 test environments, METTA achieves a success rate over $50\%$ while maintaining a low training budget and short wall-clock time. On long-context sparse-reward PointMaze tasks, it outperforms transformer-based baselines by exhibiting more structured exploration behavior. These results show that METTA provides an efficient path toward more adaptive and scalable long-context meta-RL.

candidates.title: Accelerated Execution of Bayesian Neural Networks using a Single Probabilistic Forward Pass and Code Generation
candidates.abstract: Machine learning models excel across applications like medical diagnostics, weather forecasting, natural language processing and autonomous driving, yet their inadequate handling of uncertainty remains crucial for safety-critical applications. Traditional neural networks fail to recognize out-of-domain (OOD) data, often producing incorrect predictions without indicating uncertainty. Bayesian neural networks (BNNs) offer a principled framework for uncertainty estimation by providing statistically grounded probabilities alongside predictions. Despite these advantages, BNNs suffer from high computational costs in both training and prediction. Predictions require sampling over weight distributions and multiple forward passes. To address this challenge, the Probabilistic Forward Pass (PFP) serves as an extreme approximation of Stochastic Variational Inference (SVI). While SVI assumes Gaussian-distributed weights without restrictions on activations, PFP extends this assumption to activations. This enables a fully analytical uncertainty propagation, replacing multiple forward passes with a single, more complex forward pass operating on probability distributions. Thus, PFP requires specialized Gaussian-propagating operators absent from standard deep learning libraries. We present an end-to-end pipeline for training, compilation, optimization, and deployment of PFP-based BNNs on embedded ARM CPUs. By implementing custom operators in the deep learning compiler TVM, we develop a dedicated operator library for multilayer perceptrons and convolutional neural networks. Multiple operator implementations, along with manual and automatic tuning techniques, are applied to maximize efficiency. Ablation studies show that PFP consistently outperforms SVI in computational efficiency. For small mini-batch sizes, critical for low-latency applications, our approach achieves speedups of up to 3900 ×. Our results show that PFP-based BNNs achieve performance comparable to SVI-BNNs for uncertainty disentanglement on the Dirty-MNIST dataset and for complex OOD detection on CIFAR-10 against SVHN, all while significantly reducing computational overhead. These findings underscore the potential of combining Bayesian approximations with code generation and operator tuning to accelerate BNN predictions and enable their efficient deployment on resource-constrained embedded systems.

candidates.title: Direct Pass@$k$ Optimization for Thought Pruning: Balancing Quality and Diversity in Test-Time Reasoning
candidates.abstract: Test-time scaling has emerged as a key inference strategy for reasoning models, where a model generates a large number of candidate solutions in the hope of finding at least one correct solution. Running all candidate solutions to completion can be computationally demanding, so recent work prunes the candidate pool after generating only a short prefix, committing further computation only to the surviving candidates. Existing pruning strategies divide broadly into two categories: Quality-based methods assign a score to each partial solution and discard those predicted to ultimately lead to an incorrect final solution, while diversity-based methods select partial solutions that follow different reasoning trajectories and are therefore likely to cover different final solutions. The tension between these two objectives is an instance of exploration versus exploitation, yet little to no prior work on pruning exposes this trade-off directly, let alone optimizes it. In this paper, we introduce a pruning procedure that addresses this trade-off directly by optimizing pass@$k$ over the selected solution pool. In particular, it chooses the pool to maximize the probability that at least one of its partial solutions, when continued to completion, yields a correct answer. Because this objective simultaneously rewards high-quality partial solutions and penalizes redundancy among them, quality and diversity are naturally balanced by the criterion itself rather than through separate ad-hoc design choices. On eight open-weight reasoning models, our method outperforms existing quality-based and diversity-based pruning strategies. The gains are particularly pronounced when the pruning procedure keeps a moderate number of partial solutions for continued generation, highlighting the value of directly balancing quality and diversity during pruning.

candidates.title: SpectralCanary: Embarrassingly Simple Low-Frequency Traces for T2I Dataset-Use Auditing
candidates.abstract: Auditing whether a text-to-image (T2I) model was fine-tuned on a particular image collection is difficult: a model can absorb collection-level visual characteristics without reproducing training images. Proactive dataset-use auditing plants a shared signal in a dataset before release, then later checks whether that signal appears in a suspect model's generated outputs. Existing approaches often trade off verifiability, fidelity, robustness, and deployability. We introduce $\textbf{SpectralCanary}$, which uses a smooth low-pass mask to blend a fixed canary image into every collection image while leaving captions unchanged and requiring neither auxiliary generation nor per-image optimization. A lightweight verifier detects the transferred signal in suspect-model outputs. Across eight tests on the Pokemon dataset and three realistic data transformations, spanning two architectures families, SpectralCanary achieves the highest average per-generation TPR@$1\%$ FPR ($91.1\%$) and fixed threshold model-level accuracy using 30 generations ($94.8\%$) among the evaluated methods. Across five datasets spanning artistic, medical, satellite, and fashion domains with SD3.5, SpectralCanary averages $92.4\%$ per-generation TPR@$1\%$ FPR while preserving the released images (SSIM $0.989$, LPIPS $0.022$) with a near-zero mean change FID (mean $Δ$FID $0.05$) across datasets. Matched-energy ablations on Pokemon and ROCOv2 support our design choice, low-frequency placement transfers more reliably compared to mid/high-frequency placement. Under the evaluated adaptive attacks, the most effective removal requires aggressive modification and incurs more than $25$ $Δ$FID points. These results identify low-frequency visual signals as effective carriers for collection-level T2I audit traces.

candidates.title: Behavioral Mapping of Hierarchical Dynamical Models Accelerates Bayesian Parameter Inference
candidates.abstract: Bayesian parameter inference for complex nonlinear dynamical models is often limited by the cost of repeated model simulation. We present a behavioral mapping framework that uses the inferred posterior of a higher-level model to accelerate inference of a lower-level model without requiring state or parameter correspondence between them. Building on approximate simulation relations for hierarchically related models, we define the notion of behavioral compatibility and quantify the behavioral support of detailed model parameters using the reduced model posterior. We learn a level set of behavioral support using a Gaussian process and use it to filter detailed model parameter proposals before expensive simulations during Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) inference. We derive conditions under which the behavioral support level set retains all detailed model parameters that fit the experimental data within a prescribed tolerance. We apply this method to a hierarchy of gene-expression models fitted to cell-free experimental data. After initial setup costs, our approach speeds up MCMC by 8.02% for the phenomenological model and 15.21% for the mechanistic model.

candidates.title: Fast and accurate resolution of ecDNA sequence using Cycle-Extractor
candidates.abstract: Extrachromosomal DNA (ecDNA) plays a key role in cancer pathology. EcDNAs mediate high oncogene amplification and expression and worse patient outcomes. Accurately determining the structure of these circular molecules is essential for understanding their function, yet reconstructing ecDNA cycles from sequencing data remains challenging. We introduce Cycle-Extractor (CE) for reconstruction. CE accepts a breakpoint graph derived from either short or long read sequencing data as input and extracts a cycle with the maximum length-weighted-copy-number. CE utilizes a mixed-integer linear program (MILP) and a separate traversal procedure, enabling fast optimization and compatibility with free solvers. We evaluated CE against CoRAL (long-read-based quadratic optimization), Decoil (long-reads), and AmpliconArchitect (AA for short reads) on both simulated data and real cancer cell lines. On simulated ecDNA, CE achieves performance comparable to CoRAL across three accuracy metrics and consistently outperforms AA and Decoil. On cancer cell lines, CE produces longer and heavier cycles than AA, and achieves performance similar to CoRAL. Moreover, CE is, on average, 40 x faster than CoRAL. These results demonstrate that CE accurately reconstructs ecDNA from both short- and long-read sequencing data, while long-read inputs allow CE to recover more complete and higher-confidence ecDNA structures. CE improved the prediction of many ecDNA structures. On a PC3 ecDNA containing MYC, CE uses ONT data to reconstruct a substantially larger and higher-copy sequence (4.2 Mbp) compared to the short-read-derived reconstruction (690 Kbp). CRISPR-CATCH experiments confirm the presence of a large ecDNA molecule, validating the long-read-based CE reconstruction.

candidates.title: Functional characterization of a MatE transporter in Methermicoccus shengliensis and evolutionary diversity of archaeal MatE transporters
candidates.abstract: Archaea, one of the three domains of life, exhibit remarkable physiological diversity and occupy a wide spectrum of ecological niches, ranging from extreme environments such as hypersaline lakes, hot springs, and acidic or alkaline habitats to moderate ecosystems including marine, freshwater, terrestrial, oilfield and host-associated environments. Among them, methanogenic archaea are obligate anaerobes that produce methane through distinct methanogenic pathways, traditionally utilizing simple substrates such as H2/CO2, acetate, methanol, and methylated compounds. The recent discovery that Methermicoccus shengliensis can metabolize methoxylated aromatic compounds (MACs) has expanded the known substrate spectrum of methanogens. However, the molecular mechanisms underlying the transport of these structurally complex compounds into archaeal cells remain unknown. In this study, we investigated the substrate transport system of M. shengliensis ZC-1 cultivated with methanol and 2-methoxybenzoate. Transcriptomic analysis identified two highly expressed genes, matE and tlp, potentially involved in substrate uptake. Integrating bioinformatic analyses, protein-protein interaction, and structural modeling assays, we propose a transport model comprising three sequential steps: the transduction like protein Tlp first recognizes the 2-methoxybenzoate extracellularly, then interacts with the transmembrane MATE family transporter MatE, and finally MatE mediates the translocation of the substrate into the cell. Deletion of MatE markedly impairs cell growth and methane production under methoxylated aromatic conditions, underscoring its critical role in methoxydotrophic methanogenesis. To further elucidate the diversity and habitat adaptation of archaeal MatE transporters, we performed large-scale comparative genomic phylogenetic analyses, combined with structural classification and molecular docking. Our results reveal that MatE transporters are widely distributed but unevenly represented across archaeal lineages, exhibiting structural diversity that can be classified into four major classes. Class I MatE is the most conserved and phylogenetically prevalent, whereas Classes II, III, and IV are comparatively rare. Notably, compared with MatE-negative genomes, MatE-positive archaeal genomes are significantly enriched in host-associated and hypersaline environments, as well as in heterotrophic lineages. Furthermore, specific MatE transporters exhibit strong associations with particular habitats, and their copy numbers are positively correlated with genome size. This non-random distribution indicates that the presence of MatE transporters is closely linked to specific ecological niches and metabolic strategies. Overall, this work uncovers a previously uncharacterized transport mechanism for methoxylated aromatic compounds in methanogenic archaea and provides a comprehensive framework for understanding the diversity and habitat adaptation of the archaeal MATE transporter family. These findings advance our understanding of substrate acquisition strategies and methane metabolism in archaea, provide new insights into their ecological distribution, and elucidate their adaptation to extreme environments, highlighting their biological importance and deepening our understanding of life on Earth.

candidates.title: Bayesian Variable Selection Approaches to Identifying Selection in Evolutionary Datasets
candidates.abstract: We consider the problem of identifying individual sites and characters under selection in phylogenetic datasets. We introduce an approach based on the application of Bayesian variable selection to mutation-selection models, which enables both sites and selection coefficients to be explicitly excluded from the model in order to control parameter complexity. We provide an accelerated Gibbs sampling algorithm for model selection and parameter estimation, which enables our approach to scale to realistic sequence lengths and dataset sizes. We compare this approach to previous models that do not produce sparse solutions but attempt to control complexity through Dirichlet-process (DP) mixture model prior distributions. We demonstrate that the Bayesian variable selection approach outperforms the DP approach for a wide range of settings and selection signal strengths, while offering additional advantages of sparsity and interpretability. We also identify a problem of the DP prior producing "phantom selection" artifacts, on both simulated and real datasets, which the Bayesian variable selection approach avoids.

candidates.title: High-fidelity bispecific protease KRysin for deeper plasma proteomics and phosphoproteomics
candidates.abstract: Bottom-up proteomics relies on efficient and reproducible proteolytic digestion. Yet trypsin, the most widely used protease, frequently misses cleavages, particularly near prolines, acidic and phosphorylated residues. Incomplete digestion inflates search space, dilutes peptide signal, and limits depth and reproducibility, especially in challenging matrices such as plasma and phosphoproteomics. Here we present KRysin, a recombinant bispecific protease that cleaves C-terminal to lysine and arginine with very high specificity and efficiency, generating tryptic peptides compatible with standard proteomics workflows. In HeLa digests, ~99% of KRysin-generated peptides ended in lysine or arginine, including at sites followed by proline, and only 0.2% of peptides contained an internal (missed-cleaved) arginine and 6% an internal lysine, compared with 9% and 25%, respectively, for trypsin. Using narrow-window DIA at 60 samples-per-day, KRysin quantified close to 50,000 class I phosphosites, >10,000 more than trypsin-based workflows, and identified up to 40% more plasma protein groups, uniquely revealing receptors, cytokines, and growth factors. KRysin therefore provides a direct alternative to trypsin wherever digestion completeness, speed and PTM coverage are limiting.

candidates.title: Robust multi-weather UAV small object detection framework with complex entropy-aware and wavelet convolution
candidates.abstract: Abstract In adverse weather conditions such as fog, haze, rain, and snow, unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) small object detection faces decreased accuracy due to reduced image quality and blurred object features, which seriously affects the reliability of low-altitude detection tasks. To address this challenge, this paper proposes a robust multi-weather UAV small object detection framework based on unsupervised domain adaptation with a teacher-student self-training paradigm. The proposed framework introduces complex entropy-aware attention and wavelet convolution to enhance target representation under severe weather degradation. Aiming at the domain distribution differences in multi-weather scenarios, the framework alleviates such differences through more robust category-level prototype matching and global statistical characteristic learning based on DATR (domain adaptive detection transformer model). First, to alleviate feature uncertainty introduced by adverse weather noise, we design a complex entropy-aware attention mechanism that estimates channel-wise Shannon entropy and assigns adaptive weights according to feature information concentration. Instead of simply emphasizing uncertain responses, the proposed mechanism suppresses high-entropy ambiguous features while preserving low-entropy discriminative representations that remain more reliable under weather-induced degradation. Next, to solve the limitations of traditional convolution in capturing the global context of small objects and distinguishing objects from noise, we propose to use wavelet convolution to leverage frequency-domain multi-scale decomposition and large receptive fields, strengthening the capture of global context for small objects and improving the distinction between objects and noise through frequency filtering. Finally, to further improve the stability of teacher model evolution under cross-weather domain shifts, we design a grouped EMA (exponential moving average) strategy. Unlike conventional Mean Teacher or BYOL frameworks that employ a globally fixed decay coefficient, the proposed strategy dynamically adjusts grouped parameter updating rates according to feature adaptation requirements, providing a more flexible optimization trajectory for domain adaptation. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed framework improves UAV small object detection performance under several adverse weather domain-shift scenarios, while showing promising robustness against weather-induced feature degradation.

candidates.title: Multi-criteria prioritized reinforcement learning for autonomous underwater vehicle navigation in 3D multi-node environments
candidates.abstract: Abstract Autonomous underwater vehicles (AUVs) are increasingly used as mobile data collectors in underwater wireless sensor networks, where navigation must balance task completion, obstacle avoidance, communication performance, and energy efficiency. This study develops a Twin Delayed Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient framework with Multi-Criteria Prioritized Experience Replay (MC-PER-TD3). The replay priority combines normalized temporal-difference error with a goal-proximity heuristic; energy consumption is incorporated into the reward and data-collection evaluation rather than the replay priority. A soft potential-field reward and a time-window-based waypoint escape-transition mechanism are further used to guide continuous navigation. Across six training seeds and 60 deterministic-policy evaluation episodes per seed, MC-PER-TD3 achieved 100% mission success with zero observed collisions. Relative to uniform-replay TD3, the mean successful path length decreased from 13.188 ± 3.885 m to 10.985 ± 0.436 m and task time from 6.911 ± 1.511 s to 5.654 ± 0.257 s. A standard TD-error-only PER-TD3 baseline achieved 50% mission success, whereas the combined TD-error-plus-goal replay achieved consistent completion across all six training seeds. Additional zero-shot tests under observation noise, current perturbations, fixed and randomized obstacle layouts reveal condition-dependent robustness and clear failure boundaries. In UWSN evaluation, MC-PER-TD3 achieved the highest mean energy efficiency, while TD3 retained the highest throughput, indicating a throughput-energy trade-off rather than universal dominance.

candidates.title: Economic lifetime-aware wind farm control
candidates.abstract: Abstract. We present the economic lifetime-aware formulation of wind farm control (WFC), a novel approach that incorporates the current state of damage of turbines – either provided by a digital twin or estimated from operational data – to compute control policies that optimize the long-term life management of a wind farm. The optimization is guided by an economic value function that balances power capture (taking into account variable spot market prices) with operation and maintenance (O&M) costs, including potential revenue losses due to turbine downtime. The optimization process is subject to constraints ensuring that the target lifetime of selected turbine components is met, considering varying inflow conditions. This results in optimal control setpoints for each turbine as functions of ambient conditions. After introducing the economic lifetime-aware WFC approach, the paper analyzes two case studies. The first is a synthetic scenario with a simplified set of environmental conditions, designed to demonstrate the behavior of the new control strategy and its impact on fatigue loads. The second case features the more realistic setup of a small wind farm, with wind climate data derived from a real meteorological mast. The benefits of the proposed methodology are highlighted by comparing it to a range of reference control strategies, which either ignore component damage or address fatigue loads in alternative simplified ways. When compared to greedy and power-maximizing WFC strategies, results show that only the lifetime-aware formulation ensures the achievement of the desired lifetime targets. Additionally, it also results in the best economic performance.
